questions.stem: Consider a file of size 4 million bytes being transferred between two hosts connected via a path consisting of three consecutive links of bandwidth 2 Mbps, 500 kbps, and 1 Mbps, respectively. All processing delays and propagation delays are negligible. Assume that there is no other background traffic over the path and no other additional overhead to transfer the file. Which one of the following is the total time (in seconds) to transfer the file? Note: 1M=$10^6$, 1k=$10^3$

solutionDiagram.alt: Three links in series with their transfer times; the 500 kbps link takes 64 seconds and sets the total

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: Bandwidth is how many bits a link can push out each second. Delay from distance (propagation) is stated to be zero here, so the only delay is the time bits spend being pushed onto links. A file crosses links in series as a stream: bits already through a fast link wait at the node in front of a slower link, but the slower link never sits idle once it starts. So the transfer time of a long stream is set by the slowest link (the bottleneck): total time = file size / smallest bandwidth.

steps.title: Convert the file to bits
steps.body: Bandwidth is in bits per second and the file is in bytes, so multiply by 8. The file is $4\times10^6$ bytes, which is 32 million bits.

steps.title: Time on each link alone
steps.body: Dividing the bits by each link's rate gives how long that link needs: 16 s on 2 Mbps, 64 s on 500 kbps, 32 s on 1 Mbps. The slowest link, 500 kbps, needs the most time.

steps.title: Total time
steps.body: The faster links finish their work inside the 64 s window of the bottleneck (the last link must wait to receive bits but is never the limit, and with negligible delay the first bits arrive instantly), so the file is complete after 64 s. This matches option B.

shortcut.body: Find the smallest rate (500 kbps), convert 4 MB to 32 Mbit and divide: 32 / 0.5 = 64. About 30 seconds. This is safe because propagation and processing delays are zero; with a large per-packet store-and-forward delay it would not be.

traps.text: 731 would come from mis-scaling units, for example treating bytes as bits or mixing kilo and mega. Always convert to bits first.
8 divides 4 million by 500 thousand, mixing bytes with a rate in bits and so missing the factor 8.
16 is the time on the fastest link (2 Mbps) alone. The file cannot move faster than the slowest link allows.

recognize.clues: Three links in series with different bandwidths, a file size given in bytes, and all propagation and processing delays stated as negligible. Only rates and size are left to use.
recognize.contrast: Store-and-forward pipelining (store-and-forward topic) matters when packets are small and each hop adds a packet time; here the stream is one long transfer and the bottleneck rate alone sets the time.

check.body: Work backwards from the answer: at the bottleneck rate of 500 kbps, 64 s carries $64\times5\times10^{5}=3.2\times10^{7}$ bits, which is exactly the file size. At 16 s the bottleneck link could have carried only $8\times10^{6}$ bits, a quarter of the file, so 16 s is too short.

hints.text: The file passes through three links one after another. Which of them limits how fast the stream as a whole can move?
Bits already through a fast link queue up at the node in front of a slower one. A slow link never has to wait once bits are lined up for it.
With propagation and processing delays zero, a long stream is paced by its narrowest link, so only that link's rate matters for the total time.
Convert the file from bytes to bits first, because the rates are in bits per second, then divide by the rate of the narrowest link.
Write the three rates in bits per second and pick out the smallest one.

variation.stem: A file of 3 million bytes is sent over a path of three consecutive links with bandwidths 4 Mbps, 600 kbps and 2 Mbps. Propagation and processing delays are negligible and there is no other traffic. How long, in seconds, does the transfer take? (1M = $10^6$, 1k = $10^3$)
variation.explanation: The file is $3\times10^6\times8=2.4\times10^7$ bits. The narrowest link is 600 kbps, so the time is $2.4\times10^7/6\times10^5=40$ s. 5 forgets the factor 8, 12 uses the 2 Mbps link, and 58 adds the three single-link times.

questions.stem:
Identify the ONE CORRECT matching between the OSI layers and their corresponding functionalities as shown.

OSI Layers: (a) Network layer, (b) Transport layer, (c) Datalink layer.
Functionalities: (I) Packet routing, (II) Framing and error handling, (III) Host to host communication

solutionDiagram.alt: Network layer to packet routing, transport layer to host to host communication, data link layer to framing and error handling

steps.title: What a layer is
steps.body: A network is built in layers; each layer does one job for the layer above it and uses the layer below. The OSI model names seven. Three matter here: the data link layer moves bits between two machines on the same link, the network layer moves packets across many links to the destination machine, and the transport layer carries data between programs running on the two end hosts.

steps.title: Data link layer
steps.body: It cuts the bit stream into frames (framing) and detects or corrects transmission errors on one link. So (c) matches (II).

steps.title: Network layer
steps.body: It chooses the path a packet takes through routers (routing) and addresses hosts. So (a) matches (I).

steps.title: Transport layer
steps.body: It provides communication between the two end hosts (end to end, host to host), using ports and, for TCP, reliability. So (b) matches (III). The set is (a)-(I), (b)-(III), (c)-(II), which is option B.

shortcut.body: Link layer means frames, network layer means routing, so (a)-(I) and (c)-(II) already force option B. Under 30 seconds.

traps.text: Pairs transport with framing and link with host-to-host; frames are a link-layer idea, not an end-to-end one.

Gives framing to the network layer and routing to the transport layer. Frames exist on a single link, so framing belongs to the data link layer, and routing across links belongs to the network layer. It also gives host-to-host to the data link layer, which only reaches the next machine on the same link.
Gives host-to-host to the network layer and routing to the link layer. Routing needs a global view of paths, which the link layer lacks.

recognize.clues: The question names OSI layers and asks for a one-to-one match with functions. Words like framing, routing and host to host each point at a different layer.
recognize.contrast: Data link versus transport: both can handle errors, but the link layer does it for one hop between neighbours, while transport does it between the two end hosts across the whole path.

check.body: Follow one packet through a router. The router strips the old frame and builds a new one for the next link, yet the packet's destination address is untouched and still steers every router along the way. Framing is therefore redone per link while routing uses the packet's end-to-end destination, and only the two end hosts take part in the host-to-host exchange.

hints.text: For each layer, ask how far its job reaches: one link, a whole path of routers, or the two end programs?
The OSI model stacks layers, and each one serves the layer above using the layer below. Each has a narrow job of its own.
Each layer's job reaches a different distance: some work only between two neighbouring machines, some across the whole path, and some only at the two end programs. Ask which job needs which reach.
Match the two functions that are easiest to place first, then see which description is left for the remaining layer.

variation.stem: Match each OSI layer with its function. Layers: (a) Transport layer, (b) Data link layer, (c) Physical layer. Functions: (I) sending raw bits as signals over the medium, (II) delivering data between programs on two end hosts, (III) framing and error detection on a link. Which ONE matching is correct?
variation.explanation: The physical layer moves raw bits as signals, so (c)-(I). The data link layer builds frames and detects errors on one link, so (b)-(III). That leaves the transport layer with end-to-end delivery between programs, (a)-(II).

questions.stem:
Consider a network path P—Q—R between nodes P and R via router Q. Node P sends a file of size $10^6$ bytes to R via this path by splitting the file into chunks of $10^3$ bytes each. Node P sends these chunks one after the other without any wait time between the successive chunk transmissions. Assume that the size of extra headers added to these chunks is negligible, and that the chunk size is less than the MTU.

Each of the links P—Q and Q—R has a bandwidth of $10^6$ bits/sec, and negligible propagation latency. Router Q immediately transmits every packet it receives from P to R, with negligible processing and queueing delays. Router Q can simultaneously receive on link P—Q and transmit on link Q—R.

Assume P starts transmitting the chunks at time $t = 0$. Which one of the following options gives the time (in seconds, rounded off to 3 decimal places) at which R receives all the chunks of the file?

solutionDiagram.alt: Two timelines: P to Q busy from 0 to 8.000 s, Q to R busy from 0.008 to 8.008 s

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: Transmission time is packet size divided by link rate: the time to push every bit of the packet onto the wire. A router that uses store-and-forward waits until a whole packet has arrived, then sends it on. If it can receive the next packet while sending the previous one, the two links work in parallel (pipelining), so the file time is the time to send everything on the first link plus the time to forward just the last packet on the second.

steps.title: Time for one chunk
steps.body: A chunk is 1000 bytes = 8000 bits, and the rate is $10^6$ bit/s.

steps.title: First link
steps.body: The file has $10^6/10^3=1000$ chunks, sent back to back. P finishes the last chunk at $1000\times0.008=8.000$ s, and Q has it fully by then (no propagation delay).

steps.title: Second link
steps.body: Chunk $k$ arrives at Q at $0.008k$ and is forwarded at once, so Q to R is always one chunk behind P to Q. The last chunk leaves Q at 8.000 and reaches R after one more chunk time of 0.008 s.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: 8.008 s is option B. Without pipelining the time would be 16.000 s.

shortcut.body: Pipelined store-and-forward over h links with n equal packets: (n + h - 1) packet times = (1000 + 1) x 8 ms = 8.008 s. About 1 minute. Valid only when the link rates are equal and delays are negligible.

traps.text: 8.000 forgets that Q must receive the final chunk completely before forwarding it, which costs one more chunk time.
15.992 is 16 - 0.008, an arithmetic slip from subtracting a chunk time when the whole-file model is used.
16.000 treats Q as waiting for the entire file before sending (whole-file store-and-forward), ignoring that Q can receive and transmit simultaneously.

recognize.clues: A path through one router, a file split into equal chunks, negligible propagation and processing delay, and the statement that the router can receive and transmit at the same time.
recognize.contrast: Delay components (delay-components topic) cover one packet on one link. Here many packets overlap on two links, so the pipeline count (n + h - 1) applies rather than a plain sum.

check.body: Take 2 chunks instead of 1000. The router receives chunk 1 by $t$, chunk 2 by $2t$, and sends chunk 2 on until $3t$. The formula with n = 2 and 2 links gives 3 chunk times, so the pattern matches. Also, the result must exceed the first-link time (8.000 s) and stay below sending the whole file twice.

hints.text: Can the second link start sending before the first link has finished sending the whole file?
A store-and-forward router must hold a whole chunk before it passes that chunk on, but it can already be receiving the next one.
When both links work at the same time, the links overlap in a pipeline, and only the last chunk has to pay for the extra hop.
Find the time for one chunk on one link, count the chunks, and ask how many chunk times pass before the last chunk is fully at R.
One chunk is 8000 bits on a $10^6$ bit/s link, and the file splits into 1000 chunks. Work out the chunk time, then decide how many chunk times the last chunk needs in total.

variation.stem: Node P sends a file of 500,000 bytes to node S over the path P-Q-R-S, split into chunks of 500 bytes sent back to back. Each of the three links has bandwidth $2\times10^6$ bits/sec and negligible propagation delay. Routers Q and R forward each chunk immediately after receiving it, with no processing or queueing delay, and can receive and transmit simultaneously. At what time, in seconds, does S receive the whole file?
variation.explanation: A chunk is 4000 bits, so one chunk time is $4000/(2\times10^6)=0.002$ s, and there are 1000 chunks. With a pipeline of n = 1000 chunks over h = 3 links, the time is $(n+h-1)\times0.002=1002\times0.002=2.004$ s. 2.000 ignores the extra hops, 2.002 counts only two links, and 6.000 sends the whole file one hop at a time.

questions.stem: Consider a 100 Mbps link between an earth station (sender) and a satellite (receiver) at an altitude of 2100 km. The signal propagates at a speed of $3\times10^{8}$ m/s. The time taken (in milliseconds, rounded off to two decimal places) for the receiver to completely receive a packet of 1000 bytes transmitted by the sender is_________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Timeline: 0.08 ms to transmit the packet plus 7 ms of travel gives 7.08 ms

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: Transmission delay is the time to push all bits of a packet onto the link: packet length divided by bandwidth. Propagation delay is the time one bit needs to travel the distance: distance divided by signal speed. The receiver has the whole packet only when the last bit has been sent and has also travelled across, so total = transmission + propagation.

steps.title: Transmission delay
steps.body: 1000 bytes = 8000 bits at $10^8$ bit/s.

steps.title: Propagation delay
steps.body: The distance is the altitude, 2100 km = $2.1\times10^{6}$ m.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: Add the two: 0.08 + 7 = 7.08 ms, inside the accepted range 7.07 to 7.09.

shortcut.body: Propagation 2100/300000 s = 7 ms dominates; add 8000/100 us = 0.08 ms. Answer 7.08 in about 1 minute.

traps.text: 7.00 forgets transmission time of the packet.
0.08 gives only the transmission delay and ignores the distance.
14.08 doubles the propagation delay as for a round trip, but the question asks only for one-way reception.

recognize.clues: A packet size in bytes, a bandwidth in Mbps, a distance and a signal speed, with a request for the time until the receiver has completely received the packet.
recognize.contrast: Throughput-bdp covers how much data fits in flight on a link; here we want the time for one packet, which is transmission delay plus propagation delay.

check.body: Second route through the bandwidth-delay product: in 7 ms the link holds $7\times10^{-3}\times10^{8}=7\times10^{5}$ bits, far more than the 8000-bit packet. So the packet is a tiny sliver of the pipe, its transmission time must be a small fraction of the propagation time, and the total must sit just above 7 ms.

hints.text: What must have happened before the receiver holds the whole packet, and which two separate delays add up to that?
Pushing the bits onto the link takes time, and then the signal still has to travel the distance. These two delays depend on different quantities.
Transmission delay is size over bandwidth. Propagation delay is distance over signal speed. The last bit has arrived only after both have passed.
Convert 1000 bytes to bits and the altitude to metres, compute each delay in seconds, then add them and express the sum in milliseconds.

variation.stem: A 50 Mbps link joins a ground station to a satellite at an altitude of 1500 km. The signal speed is $3\times10^8$ m/s. How long, in milliseconds, does the satellite take to completely receive a packet of 500 bytes sent by the station? Round to two decimal places.
variation.explanation: Transmission delay is $4000/(5\times10^7)=0.08$ ms. Propagation delay is $1.5\times10^6/(3\times10^8)=5$ ms. The packet is fully received after their sum, 5.08 ms.

questions.stem: Consider two hosts $X$ and $Y$, connected by a single direct link of rate $10^6$ bits/sec. The distance between the two hosts is 10,000 km and the propagation speed along the link is $2\times10^{8}$ m/sec. Host $X$ sends a file of 50,000 bytes as one large message to host $Y$ continuously. Let the transmission and propagation delays be $p$ milliseconds and $q$ milliseconds, respectively. Then the values of $p$ and $q$ are

solutionDiagram.alt: Timeline: 400 ms to transmit the file, then 50 ms propagation

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: Transmission delay is the time to put all bits of the message onto the link: message size in bits divided by the link rate. Propagation delay is the time a signal takes to cross the link: distance divided by propagation speed. They depend on different quantities (size and rate, versus distance and speed), so compute them separately.

steps.title: Transmission delay p
steps.body: 50,000 bytes = 400,000 bits at $10^6$ bit/s.

steps.title: Match
steps.body: p = 400 and q = 50 is option D.

shortcut.body: Compute only p = 400,000 / 10^6 = 0.4 s = 400 ms. Only option D has p = 400. Under 1 minute.

traps.text: Gives p=50 and q=100: p=50 is 400 divided by 8, a double slip with bytes and bits, and q is wrong too.
Swaps p and q: it uses distance over speed for transmission and size over rate for propagation.
q=50 is right, but p=100 is wrong: the file takes 400 ms to send, not 100.

recognize.clues: The question asks for transmission delay p and propagation delay q separately, and gives a file size, a link rate, a distance and a propagation speed.
recognize.contrast: Do not mix them up: p comes from size and rate, q from distance and speed. A swapped pair is one of the listed options.

check.body: Recheck the units with the inputs reordered. Size: $50000\times8=4\times10^{5}$ bits, and $4\times10^{5}/10^{6}=0.4$ s. Distance: $10{,}000\text{ km}=10^{7}$ m, and $10^{7}/(2\times10^{8})=0.05$ s. Converting 0.4 s and 0.05 s to milliseconds gives 400 and 50, and only option D lists that pair.

hints.text: The question asks for two different delays. What does each one depend on: the message, the link, or the distance?
Transmission delay is the time to put the message onto the wire. Propagation delay is the time the signal needs to cross the wire.
Transmission delay uses message size and link rate. Propagation delay uses distance and propagation speed. Neither one uses the other's inputs.
Convert bytes to bits and kilometres to metres. Compute each delay in seconds, then convert to milliseconds before matching with the options.

variation.stem: Hosts A and B are joined by one direct link of rate $2\times10^6$ bits/sec. They are 6000 km apart and the signal travels at $2\times10^8$ m/sec. A sends a file of 25,000 bytes as one message. Let the transmission and propagation delays be p ms and q ms. Which pair gives p and q?
variation.explanation: The file has 200,000 bits, so $p=200000/(2\times10^6)=0.1$ s = 100 ms. The distance is $6\times10^6$ m, so $q=6\times10^6/(2\times10^8)=0.03$ s = 30 ms. The pair 30 and 100 swaps them, 12.5 treats bytes as bits, and 60 doubles q as if for a round trip.
